business-management/04-market/04-2-buyer.title: 04-2 Buyers, Sellers, and the Space Between Them
business-management/04-market/04-2-buyer.description:
Part of 04 MarketYou've already met the market as an arena where a good or service gets bought and sold. But an arena isn't just a floor — it's full of people. Two kinds, in fact: the people who want to buy, the people who want to sell, and a surprising amount of machinery standing in between them. That in-between part is where most of the money, and most of the strategy, actually lives.Start with the buyer. A buyer has a need, some money, limited time, limited information, and a set of alternatives. Their private question is simple: is this worth it, compared with everything else I could do with this money?Now the seller. A seller has something to offer, a cost base, a capacity limit, and — this is the part beginners skip — a need to sell enough of it to cover the costs of making it at all. Their private question is: can I sell this at a price that leaves something over?Both sides are trying to read a person they can't fully see. Economists call this information asymmetry, and it's the reason markets are never as clean as the diagrams suggest. Priya knows exactly when her bread came out of the oven; you don't. You know exactly how much you're willing to pay; she doesn't.One more thing worth noticing early: almost everyone is both. Priya sells loaves and buys flour, butter, electricity and cardboard boxes. So does the industrial baker down the road, and so does the supermarket she sells to. Whenever you think about a market, ask which side of it am I standing on right now? — because the same person can be a seller in one transaction and a buyer in the next one, five minutes later.If buying and selling were simple, a hungry person with £4 and a baker with a loaf would just find each other and swap. Often they can't, and the reasons are worth naming, because each one is a business opportunity in disguise. Space. The bakery is four miles from the office where the hunger is. Time. The flour mill harvests once a year and sells continuously; the bakery buys every week. Information. You don't know which of the twelve nearby bakeries is any good, and the good one doesn't know you exist. Trust. Will you actually pay? Will they actually deliver what was promised? Quantity and matching. The mill sells flour by the tonne. Priya needs four 16kg sacks. Neither of them wants to change their size for the other. Risk. Somebody has to buy stock before anyone has confirmed they want it — and swallow the loss if the loaves don't sell. Those gaps are the reason a market is more than a place. A market is a system that bridges them, over and over, at a cost low enough for everyone to come out ahead.Every arrow in that chain is a place where a deal can stall. Bridge all of them cheaply and you have a working market.The bridges have names. Wholesalers buy in bulk and break it into smaller amounts. Retailers put goods where buyers already are. Distributors move stock between them. Agents and brokers match buyers to sellers without ever owning the goods. Marketplaces and platforms host the whole exchange and take a cut. Banks and payment providers solve the "will you actually pay?" gap. Insurers carry the risk that something goes wrong. Logistics firms close the space gap, one van at a time.Notice that none of them make the product. They exist because closing a gap is worth money — and the reason they get paid is worth saying plainly: the middleman must be cheaper than the gap they close. If a wholesaler's markup is bigger than the cost of Priya driving to the mill herself and storing a pallet of flour in her back room, she'll drive. Middlemen are not parasites or heroes; they're a cost you accept because the alternative costs more. (The Suppliers and Distribution chapters dig into choosing and managing them properly.)This works in both directions over time. When the internet made it cheap for a bakery to reach customers directly, some intermediaries got squeezed out — disintermediation. Then a new wave appeared: delivery platforms, online marketplaces, review sites. Re-intermediation. The gap rarely closes; it just gets filled by somebody new.placeholder
Photo by Brett Sayles on PexelsHere's the puzzle at the heart of every market: you hand over money to a stranger and expect bread in return. Why does that work?Partly reputation. Brands, reviews, star ratings, "family run since 1974", a logo you recognise on a van. All of it is compressed evidence that the seller has something to lose by cheating you.Partly rules and enforcement. Contract law, consumer protection, food safety standards, weights and measures, licences, and the threat of a fine or a lawsuit. This is regulation doing its quiet job — it makes strangers safe to trade with. (The Regulations chapter takes this further; here, just note that a market without rules gets smaller, because people stop trusting it.)And partly the price, which is the most remarkable piece of information-compression ever invented: a single number that tells you, all at once, roughly how scarce something is, how much others value it, and whether you should bother. How that number gets set is the subject of the next subsection — but you can already see that it only works because all this trust and infrastructure is holding it up.placeholder
Photo by ALHawraa on PexelsPriya's bakery can make 3,000 loaves a month. Here's how she sells them, and what each route costs her.Look at the app and the wholesaler and you might think: they're skimming £1.00 and £1.40 a loaf — close them down. But try it. Her shop counter only closes the "space" gap for people who live nearby; she physically cannot sell 3,000 loaves over one counter in one month, because there aren't enough passers-by. The app closes the space and convenience gaps for customers across town; the wholesaler closes the matching and volume gaps in one meeting. Both charge for it. Both buy her something she doesn't have: reach.Now flip her to the buying side. Priya needs flour. The mill sells by the tonne at roughly £17 per 16kg sack's worth; a wholesaler delivers four sacks a week at £24 each. On paper the mill is far cheaper — but the tonne minimum would tie up about £1,000 of her cash and fill her back room with flour she'd be paying insurance on. The wholesaler's £7-per-sack premium buys her cash, space and time, and lets her order again next week at whatever volume her sales actually justify.So the honest test, in both directions, is never "is there a middleman?" It's "which gap is this middleman closing, and is it cheaper than closing it myself?"This subsection is short, but it changes how you look at your own business.First: you can compete on the gap, not just the product. Plenty of very profitable companies never make anything better than their rivals. They simply make buying easier — faster delivery, painless returns, clearer information, a stronger guarantee, a shelf in a more convenient place. Those aren't marketing gimmicks. They're real reductions in the buyer's cost of doing business with you, and customers pay for them. Keep this in mind when you reach the Stores, Distribution and Customer Service chapters; it's the thread that ties them together.Second: whoever stands between you and your customer shapes your whole business. Sell through your own shop and you keep more of the £4, control the experience, and face one set of competitors. Sell through an app or a wholesaler and you get reach, but you hand over margin and some control over pricing and service — and, as the Competitors chapter pointed out, your competitive set changes completely. Wholesale Priya is fighting industrial bakers on price and reliability, not competing with the café two doors down on atmosphere.Third: the gap is your map of opportunities. Walk through the six gaps above and ask, honestly, which one is being badly closed in your market right now. Slow delivery? Confusing information? Nobody willing to sell in the small quantities people actually want? That's usually where a small business can out-position a bigger one — not by being cheaper, but by being easier.And fourth: none of it happens by itself. Someone has to choose the channels, work out what each one really costs after commissions, check that they're producing what you expected, and change course when they aren't. That's the management loop from the opening chapter, applied to your place in the market. Good strategists don't drift into a channel because everyone else uses it — they pick it deliberately and measure what it earns.One caution before we move on. Not every gap is worth closing, and not every middleman earns their keep. Same-day delivery sounds wonderful until you work out that customers won't pay enough to cover it. A distributor you can't attach to any specific gap is probably just a cost line. The discipline is to name the gap, name the price of closing it, and compare that with what buyers will actually pay.placeholder
Photo by Nataliya Vaitkevich on Pexels Every market has buyers (needs, money, limited time and information) and sellers (a product, a cost base, a capacity limit) — and most people are both, depending on the transaction. Buyers and sellers are separated by gaps: space, time, information, trust, quantity and matching, and risk. A market is the system that bridges those gaps cheaply enough for both sides to benefit. Intermediaries — wholesalers, retailers, distributors, agents, platforms, banks, insurers, logistics — exist to close specific gaps, and they earn their keep only when they cost less than the gap they close. Trust, reputation and rules are the connective tissue that makes trading with strangers safe; prices compress all of it into one number. Strategically, you can win by closing a gap better than anyone else, and your choice of who stands between you and the buyer changes your margins, your control, and who your competitors are. The standing test: name the gap, price the fix, and check what buyers will pay. An intermediary you can't attach to a gap is just a cost. Next, we'll look at how that single number — the price — gets set by supply and demand.

business-management/04-market/04-3-how-s.title: 04-3 How Supply and Demand Set the Price
business-management/04-market/04-3-how-s.description:
Part of 04 MarketIn the last subsection you met the cast: buyers, sellers, and the space between them. Price is what fills that space. It's the number that decides whether a seller bothers to open, whether a buyer bothers to walk in, and — as you'll see — whether your business makes money or just makes noise. This subsection is about where that number actually comes from.Here's the short version, and the rest of this page unpacks it: price isn't set by you. It's set by the meeting point between what buyers want and what sellers are willing to provide. Your job as a strategist is not to announce a price but to understand that meeting point well enough to make money inside it.Start with the two sides of the space between buyers and sellers.Demand is the relationship between a price and the quantity buyers will take at that price. It slopes downwards: as the price falls, more people buy, and the people already buying buy more. This isn't a moral statement, it's arithmetic. At £2 a loaf, Sam buys two and freezes one. At £8, she buys none and makes toast at home. Nothing changed about her appetite — only the price.Supply is the relationship between a price and the quantity sellers are willing to offer. It slopes upwards, because making more usually costs more. The first hundred loaves come out of the oven during a normal shift. The next hundred need overtime, a second baker, or flour bought at short notice from a pricier supplier. This is the costs connection: each extra unit has its own cost, and a seller will only supply it if the price covers it.That's why a bakery happily bakes 200 loaves at £4 each and quietly turns the oven off at £2. Turn the price too low and the seller doesn't compete harder — they simply leave.Put the two curves together and something clean happens. At prices that are too high, sellers produce more than buyers want and stock sits unsold. At prices that are too low, buyers want more than sellers care to provide and the shelves empty. Somewhere between the two is a price where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. That's the equilibrium price, and at that price the market clears — everything made gets sold, and everyone who wanted one got one.Notice the word clears, not fair. Equilibrium says nothing about whether the price feels reasonable. It only says the two sides match.Read that loop carefully, because it's the engine of everything that follows. It isn't a committee deciding a price — it's thousands of small decisions correcting each other. Unsold bread gets discounted on Saturday afternoon. A sold-out favourite gets a price rise on Monday, or a bigger batch. The market finds the price by repeatedly overshooting and correcting. Equilibrium is a moving target, not a resting place.
Photo by Rafael Minguet Delgado on PexelsHere's where beginners trip, and where a lot of bad business decisions come from. There are two completely different things that can happen to a market, and people constantly confuse them: A movement along the curve happens when only the price itself changes. Lower the price and buyers take more; that's the same demand, described at a different point. A shift of the whole curve happens when something other than price changes — incomes, costs, tastes, taxes. Now the entire relationship changes, and the market settles at a genuinely new price and quantity. The distinction matters because only a shift creates a new opportunity or a new threat. A discount on Saturday doesn't change the market; a new office block opening down the street does.On the buyers' side, the curve moves when any of these change: Incomes. When the local economy booms, people buy more of almost everything. That's the Economy chapter showing up in your till. Taste and fashion. Sourdough becomes a status symbol; white sliced becomes a joke. Demand moves for reasons no accountant can predict. Prices of substitutes and complements. This is straight out of the Competitors chapter. If the café across the road raises its prices, your demand rises — you're substitutes. If coffee pods get cheaper, the milk people buy goes up — you're complements. The number of buyers. A new office block, a new housing estate, a cruise ship in port. Expectations. If customers think prices are about to rise, they buy now and borrow demand from next month. On the sellers' side, the curve moves when the cost of supplying changes: Input costs. A bad harvest raises the price of flour. A fuel spike raises delivery costs. Wage rises lift the cost of every hour worked. Here the Raw Materials, Labour and Suppliers chapters all feed directly into price. Technology. A better oven means more loaves from the same hours — supply shifts out, and prices tend to fall. This is one of the quiet engines of long-run prosperity. Taxes and subsidies. A new tax on sugary drinks raises the cost of supplying them; a subsidy on apprentices lowers the cost of labour. That's the Tax chapter, arriving via the supply curve. Regulation. New hygiene rules, labelling rules or licences add cost, and cost is what supply responds to. Straight from the Regulations chapter. The number of sellers. New entrants add supply. When your industry looks profitable, supply arrives and prices sag — which is exactly why good margins attract competitors.
Photo by Markus Winkler on PexelsPriya sells sourdough at £4 a loaf and bakes 100 a day, which sell out by noon. Now two things happen in one month.Shock one: a new office block opens nearby. Three hundred workers now walk past her door at lunchtime. Nothing about her bakery changed — her bread, her costs and her prices are identical. But demand has shifted. At £4, she now has a queue at 11am and sells out at 11:30. She has three options: raise the price to £4.50 and sell the same 100 to the people who really want them; bake more; or keep everything the same and disappoint customers who then try the café next door. The shift in demand gave her a decision to make — that's the whole point.Shock two: a poor harvest pushes flour up 20%. Now supply has shifted. Her cost per loaf has risen, so the price that made 100 loaves worth baking no longer does the job. She can't wish the harvest back. Her realistic choices are to charge more, shrink the loaf, cut other costs, or accept a thinner margin.Notice that neither shock came from her baking. One came from the local economy and the number of buyers; the other from raw materials and her suppliers. That's the honest lesson of supply and demand: the most important movements in your business happen outside your four walls, and the strategist's job is to see them early.There's one more idea worth carrying, because it decides whether a price rise makes you richer or poorer. Elasticity is how much the quantity bought responds to a change in price. Inelastic demand — people barely change what they buy. Insulin, salt, a train ticket to work. Raise the price and sales dip only a little. Elastic demand — people change a lot. Anything with a close substitute: bread from the bakery next door, a mid-range hotel room, a taxi versus a bus. And here's where supply and demand stops being theory and starts being your profit and loss account. Remember from the Costs chapter that each loaf has a variable cost — flour, butter, the bag — and that what's left after paying it is the contribution toward rent, wages and profit.Priya's loaf sells for £4 and costs £1.20 in ingredients. She sells 100 a day: contribution = £2.80 × 100 = £280.She tries a 10% price rise to £4.40, and 15 customers vanish:Both revenue and contribution fell. Her demand was elastic, so the price rise lost more than it gained. On a more inelastic product — say a unique celebration cake nobody else in town makes — the same 10% rise might cost her only two orders, and margin would jump. Same bakery, same arithmetic: elasticity is what decides. Cross-reference this with the Revenue chapter, because revenue is price × quantity, and they move in opposite directions.Pull it together and a few practical rules fall out. You rarely set the price; you discover it. Nearly every business is a price taker in some markets and a price maker in others. The structural reasons sit in the Types of Competition chapter; the day-to-day version is that a rival's price sets a ceiling above your head. You earn margin by shifting your own cost curve, not by arguing with the market price. In highly competitive markets, the baker who shaves two pence off the cost of a loaf keeps that two pence. Everyone else is stuck. You can change your own elasticity. Differentiate — better service, a location, a brand, a loyalty scheme — and your customers stop treating you as a straight swap for the shop next door. That's how you move away from "price is the only thing that matters". Forecast, then plan, then check. Demand shifts can be anticipated, because they leave traces: job adverts, planning applications, harvest reports, interest rate news. That's the planning and controlling loop from the management chapter applied to price. Watch the whole chain. Your suppliers' costs, your staff's wages, the taxes and rules you pay — every one of them is a supply-side shift waiting to happen.
Photo by Sara Er on Pexels Demand slopes down and supply slopes up; price is where the two meet. Nothing about either curve is a moral judgement — it's just how buyers and sellers respond. The meeting point is the equilibrium price, where the market clears. It's a moving target that markets find by repeatedly overshooting and correcting. Distinguish a movement along a curve (only the price changed) from a shift of the curve (income, costs, tastes, taxes, rivals, regulation changed). Only shifts create new opportunities and threats. Demand shifters: incomes, taste, substitute and complement prices, number of buyers, expectations. Supply shifters: input costs, technology, taxes, regulation, number of sellers. Elasticity decides whether a price rise helps you. Elastic demand means customers leave; inelastic demand means they grumble and stay. The profitability connection is direct: revenue is price × quantity, and profit depends on the contribution left after variable costs. Elasticity and cost control are what you actually control. Strategy in one line: you don't argue with the market price — you lower your costs, sharpen your differentiation, and move your own curves.

business-management/05-product/05-1-what.title: 05-1 What a Product Really Is
business-management/05-product/05-1-what.description: Part of 05 ProductMost people, asked what a product is, point at a thing: a loaf of bread, a phone, a can of paint. That answer isn't wrong, it's just the visible tenth of the idea. Get the full definition straight now and a dozen later decisions — what you charge, what it costs to make, who you sell it to, why customers come back — suddenly have a logical place to sit.A product is anything offered to a market that can satisfy a want or need — and what the customer buys is the benefit, not the object.Read that twice. The object is real, and somebody has to make it well. But the customer isn't buying flour, water and yeast bound into a crust. They're buying "something nicer than the supermarket loaf to go with Sunday breakfast", or "a treat that makes the walk to the office worth it". The loaf is the vehicle. The benefit is the purchase.This is why the Market chapter and this one lean on each other. A product only becomes a product when there's a market willing to trade for it. Invent the world's finest left-handed corkscrew in a town where nobody drinks wine and you haven't made a product — you've made an object with costs attached.The word "product" covers a lot more ground than the shelf in a shop: Goods — a bicycle, a jar of honey, a printed book. Services — a haircut, an MOT, a fortnight of accounting. Combinations, which is nearly everything. A delivered pizza is a good and a service. A software subscription is a licence plus support plus updates. “/assets/0596599aeb074814b9a63ec7c0f59bae/product_goods_placeholder.jpg” could not be found. Photo by ready made on PexelsTreat goods and services as two ends of one line rather than two categories. A hand-made chair is mostly good, with a little service — the delivery, the assembly instructions. A taxi ride is mostly service, with a little good — the car. Once you see the line, you stop asking "is this a product?" and start asking "which parts of this do I actually control?"Here's the most useful mental model in this whole chapter. Every product exists at three levels at once.The core benefit is the need being satisfied. Not "bread" but "a reliable, pleasant lunch". Not "drill" but "a hole in the wall".The actual product is the tangible version: the recipe, the size, the packaging, the label, the flavour, the way it's presented. This is what most businesses spend their time on, and rightly — it's the part you can change.The augmented product is everything wrapped around it: how easy it is to buy, how fast it arrives, whether returns are painless, the guarantee, the support, the reputation of the name on the box. In competitive markets, this is where the fight is actually won, because the actual products have converged. Two loaves of sourdough can be near-identical. One is bought from a shop that opens at 7am with a smile and a paper bag; the other from a shop with no sign and a queue out of the door.Notice how this reaches into other chapters. The augmented product is the Customer Service, Distribution and Stores chapters in disguise. When those sections talk about delivery speed, returns policy or how a shop feels, they're describing product decisions, not afterthoughts.A feature is what your product has. A benefit is what it does for the customer. Businesses fall in love with features because they're the fun part to build. Customers buy benefits and ignore everything else.The translation isn't spin. It's the difference between describing your product and describing your customer's day. If you can't put your product into a single sentence that names a benefit, you don't yet know what you're selling — and neither will anyone else.Priya bakes a sourdough loaf. Follow it through the three levels.Core benefit. Her customer, Sam, isn't solving a flour shortage. She's solving "I want fifteen good minutes and something better than the office vending machine."Actual product. The loaf itself: a 800g sourdough with a dark crust, baked at 5am, sold for £4, wrapped in paper with a hand-stamped label. Recipe, size, price, packaging, name. Every one of those is a decision somebody made.Augmented product. The shop opens at 7am so Sam can buy before work. There's a loyalty card — every tenth loaf free. Staff will slice it if she asks. If a loaf is stale when she gets it home, Priya replaces it without an argument. None of that is bread. All of it is why Sam chooses Priya's over the supermarket meal deal and the café two doors down.Now the strategic part. When Priya raised her price from £4 to £4.40 (see the Prices subsection), she didn't change the core benefit or the recipe. She was testing whether her augmented product — the reputation, the convenience, the relationship — had earned her some pricing power. That's the Competitors chapter and the Costs chapter meeting head-on: what customers will pay depends on how substitutable you are, and how substitutable you are depends on the whole bundle, not the loaf alone.Read that loop and notice something important: the product is the hinge of the whole business. Every cost you incur — raw materials, labour, manufacturing, storage, distribution — arrives at the product. Every pound of revenue leaves from it. A business is, in a very real sense, a machine for converting inputs into a product and a product into money. Get the product wrong and nothing downstream can save you.Beginners think costs are a separate topic, managed later by someone else. In truth, most of your costs are locked in the moment you define the product.Design a loaf that must be eaten within six hours and you've just signed up for fresh-baked batches, small-scale production, and waste at the end of the day. Design one that keeps for a week and your costs shift to packaging and cold chain. Choose a thick crust and you may need a different oven. Choose a delicate one and you may need different Distribution — a van that doesn't crush it.This is why the Raw Materials and Manufacturing chapters come after this one in the book. They're consequences of product decisions, not independent choices. A good strategist thinks about a product change and immediately asks: what does this do to my cost per unit, my lead times, my supplier list, my storage, and the skills my staff need?Worth separating, because the two get muddled constantly.The product is what actually gets delivered — the loaf, the app, the haircut. The brand is the set of expectations in the customer's head about what the product will be like. The brand is a promise; the product is the keeping of it.A brand can be built in years and destroyed in a week by a product that doesn't deliver. That's why consistency beats occasional brilliance. A bakery whose loaves are superb on Tuesday and mediocre on Friday has a product problem and a brand problem, and the second one is harder to fix. Start from the need, not the idea. Ask what job the customer is hiring your product to do for them. Everything else is downstream. Define the benefit in one sentence. If you can't, you don't yet know what you're selling, and neither will your staff, your suppliers, or your customers. Manage all three levels. The core benefit is settled by the customer's need, but the actual and augmented layers are where you can win. Service, delivery and returns are product decisions — the Customer Service and Distribution chapters are really about this. Remember that a product is never finished. Tastes shift, competitors move, markets shift under you. That's why the next two subsections cover the types of products and the life cycle they pass through — both are tools for deciding what to do next, not just ways of labelling what you already have. Never fall in love with the object. The world is full of beautifully made products that nobody wanted, beaten by average products sold by well-managed businesses. The market rewards the benefit delivered, not the effort spent. A product is anything offered to a market that satisfies a want or need — the customer buys the benefit, not the object. Products include goods, services and combinations; treat them as two ends of one line, not two categories. Every product has three levels: the core benefit (the need), the actual product (the tangible thing), and the augmented product (delivery, service, guarantee, brand). Competition usually happens at the third level. Features describe what you made; benefits describe what the customer gets. Always translate. The product is the hinge of the business — all costs arrive at it, all revenue leaves from it — and most costs are locked in by product decisions made early. A brand is the promise; the product is the keeping of it. Consistency is what keeps the two aligned. The test for any product decision: does this deliver more of what the customer actually needs, at a cost the business can live with?

business-management/05-product/05-2-type.title: 05-2 Types of Products
business-management/05-product/05-2-type.description:
Part of 05 ProductYou know what a product is. The next problem is that "product" covers things that behave nothing alike. A chocolate bar and a factory lathe are both products, but they're bought by different people, for different reasons, at different speeds, and they leave wildly different amounts of money behind. Sorting products into types isn't a labelling exercise — the type tells you where to sell, what to charge, how to promote, and how much margin you can realistically expect.Get the type wrong and you'll build a beautiful strategy for the wrong animal. Sell a wedding cake the way you sell a loaf of bread and you'll destroy the margin. Sell a loaf the way you sell a wedding cake and you'll lose the footfall.The single most useful split is between consumer products (bought by individuals for personal use) and business products (bought by organisations to make or sell something of their own). It's sometimes labelled B2C and B2B.The same physical object can be both. A kettle bought for a kitchen is a consumer product; a hundred kettles bought for a hotel chain are a business product. What changed isn't the kettle — it's the buyer's behaviour.That last row is worth pausing on. Derived demand means the demand for a business product comes from the demand for whatever the business is making. A café buys more bread because more people are buying sandwiches. If the café's customers stop coming, the bread order stops too — and no amount of good salesmanship on your part changes it. This is the Market chapter's supply-and-demand machinery, one step further up the chain.
Photo by Eduardo Soares on PexelsMarketers have sorted consumer products by how hard the buyer thinks about the purchase. That one variable predicts almost everything else.Convenience products are bought often, quickly, and with almost no thought. Milk, bread, chewing gum, a newspaper. The buyer's effort is tiny, so price sensitivity is high, and they'll happily swap to whatever's nearest or cheapest. That means your job is availability and habit, not persuasion: get into as many outlets as possible, keep the packaging instantly recognisable, and don't expect much of a price premium. Convenience goods tend to earn thin margins per unit and make their money on volume and repeat visits. This is why the Distribution and Stores chapters matter so much for them.Shopping products are compared before buying. Shoes, a sofa, a laptop, a family holiday. The buyer actively gathers information, weighs price against quality against style, and often visits two or three places. Here differentiation earns its keep: better service, better design, a clearer guarantee, a nicer shop. You can charge more than the shop next door — but only by as much as the buyer thinks you're genuinely different. Remember the Types of Competition chapter: this is the world of monopolistic competition, where rivals are close substitutes rather than identical goods.Specialty products are the ones the buyer will go out of their way for. A bespoke wedding cake, a particular camera lens, a specialist running shoe, a drug with no alternative. The buyer won't accept a substitute, so demand is inelastic — exactly the elasticity idea from the Market chapter. A modest price rise costs you very few sales. That's why specialty products carry the fattest margins and get sold through few, well-chosen outlets, where the brand and the expertise do the selling.Unsought products are the awkward ones: the buyer isn't looking for them. Life insurance, a will, a fire extinguisher, a dental check-up, a funeral plan. Demand has to be created rather than captured, which makes selling expensive and trust essential. Notice that unsought isn't a comment on quality. Plenty of excellent products sit here. It's a comment on the buyer's state of mind when you reach them.
Photo by Samuel Nuñez on PexelsThere's a second, quieter classification worth knowing: durable goods (used repeatedly over years — a fridge, a bike), non-durable goods (consumed quickly — a sandwich, shampoo) and services (intangible, and cannot be stored — a haircut, a repair, a night in a hotel). Services are perishable: an unsold seat on tonight's class is revenue you can never recover, which is why capacity planning and pricing-by-the-clock matter so much in service businesses.Business products sort differently, by what role they play in the buyer's operation.Raw materials and parts go into the finished product. Flour for a bakery, steel for a carmaker, a gearbox bought from a supplier. Buyers care about two things above all: reliability of supply and price per unit, because these costs sit directly inside their own margin. This is the Raw Materials and Suppliers chapters in action — and it's why business buyers often sign long contracts rather than shop around each week.Capital items are the big, long-lived purchases: buildings, ovens, delivery vans, IT systems. They're bought rarely, decided by committee, often financed with a loan, and written off over years as depreciation — which is the Financials chapter arriving through the back door. Because the sums are large and the decision is slow, capital goods are sold on negotiation, demonstration and after-sales support, not on a price tag.Supplies and services keep the place running without becoming part of the product: cleaning, stationery, lightbulbs, legal advice, accountancy, IT support. These are routine and mostly chosen on convenience and trust, which is why they're so often outsourced to the same firm for years.Two features tie all three together. Business buyers are fewer but much larger — one café contract may equal two hundred counter customers. And they're professional: they know their numbers, they ask for quotes, and they'll switch suppliers over a two pence difference if everything else is equal.
Photo by J E on PexelsA few more axes are worth keeping in your head, because each one changes the strategy. Commodity vs differentiated. A commodity is interchangeable — nobody cares whose it is, so price is the only lever and margins get squeezed. A differentiated product has a reason to be chosen, which buys pricing power. Most businesses die trying to sell a commodity as if it were differentiated. Physical vs digital. Digital products have almost no cost per extra copy, so extra sales drop straight to the bottom line. That's a completely different economics from baking, where every loaf costs flour. Regulated vs unregulated. Alcohol, medicines, financial products and food all carry licences, labelling rules and extra taxes. The Regulations and Tax chapters are not background noise for these products — they shape the packaging and the price. Branded vs own-label. The same factory output can be sold under a premium brand and under a supermarket's own label at half the price. Same product, different type in the buyer's mind. Pull it together and the classification stops being vocabulary and becomes a decision tool.Read the columns together and you can see the trap. A convenience product sold through a single boutique will fail on availability. A specialty product discounted heavily "to drive volume" throws away the very thing that made it worth buying. The type sets the rules.Priya's bakery sells six things, and each one is a different type of product needing a different approach.Same ovens, same recipes, six different games. The loaf has to be cheap and everywhere; the wedding cake has to be expensive and rare; the café contract has to be reliable rather than exciting. If Priya managed all six the same way, four of them would lose money.There's a management point here too. Her product mix — how many of each type she sells — is a planning decision, and checking how each one actually performs is the controlling half of the loop. Convenience goods supply the cash flow and the customers; specialty goods supply the margin; business contracts supply predictable volume. A good mix balances all three, and a bad mix looks busy while quietly losing money on half its range.Buyer behaviour defines the type, not your intentions. You can't declare your sandwich a specialty product by pricing it like one. Speak to your own customers: do they compare you, or do they grab and go? Their behaviour, not your label, decides what works.A product can change type. The thing that's specialty today becomes shopping when rivals copy it and convenience when everyone sells it. Types drift, usually in that direction, and the Life Cycle of a Product section picks up exactly where that drift comes from. Products sort first by who buys them: consumer products (individuals, for personal use) or business products (organisations, to make or sell something). Business demand is usually derived — it depends on the buyer's own customers, not on your sales effort. Consumer products come in four types based on how hard the buyer thinks: convenience (fast, cheap, availability-driven), shopping (compared on price and quality), specialty (no substitute accepted, high margin), and unsought (the buyer isn't looking — demand must be created). A parallel split runs by durability: durable goods, non-durable goods, and services, which are intangible and cannot be stored. Business products split into raw materials and parts, capital items, and supplies and services — with very different buying cycles, contract lengths, and financial treatment. Other useful axes: commodity vs differentiated, physical vs digital, regulated vs unregulated, branded vs own-label. The type determines where you sell, what you charge, how you promote, and how fat your margin can be — so it sits underneath decisions in the Distribution, Stores, Revenue, Costs and Customer Service chapters. Get the type right, and your whole mix earns its place: convenience brings footfall, specialty brings margin, business contracts bring volume.

business-management/05-product/05-3-the-.title: 05-3 The Life Cycle of a Product
business-management/05-product/05-3-the-.description:
Part of 05 ProductYour best-selling product will not sell forever. It gets launched, it catches on (or doesn't), it settles into a comfortable groove, and eventually something — a rival, a trend, a new technology, a change in what customers want — starts to pull it downwards. That shape, from launch to fade, is the product life cycle, and understanding it is what stops you from being surprised by your own business.The product life cycle is the pattern a product's sales and profits tend to follow over its life: introduction, growth, maturity, decline. There's also a stage before the beginning — development — where you spend money and sell nothing at all.Here's the whole thing at a glance:And here's what's actually going on in each stage:Read that table twice, because the middle columns matter more than the sales curve. A product's life cycle is really a story about competition. As a product succeeds, rivals arrive. As rivals arrive, the fight shifts from "can we make enough?" to "why should anyone pick ours?"This is the part people miss. Sales usually peak in maturity — but profit tends to peak earlier, somewhere late in growth.Three things cause the squeeze: Costs per unit fall first, then stop falling. Early on, small volumes mean every bun carries a share of the fixed costs — the oven, the rent, the staff on shift. That links straight back to the Costs chapter: fixed costs spread over few units are painful, and spreading them over many is a gift. But once you're running at capacity, the gift runs out. Prices come under pressure. As rivals multiply, your product stops being the only answer to the customer's need. In the language of the Market chapter, your demand becomes more elastic — a small price rise now costs you more customers than it did two years ago. In the language of the Competitors chapter, your market structure hardens from a crowd of small differentiated sellers into a handful of big ones fighting on everything but price. Selling costs rise. In growth, word of mouth does the work. In maturity, you're paying for it: promotions, loyalty schemes, better packaging, a nicer display. Put those together and you get the classic squeeze: more units sold, less money kept per unit.Priya adds a new product to her bakery — cinnamon buns. Watch it live through a full cycle. (Contribution here means what's left of the price after the ingredients: the money that goes toward rent, wages and profit.)Read the growth and maturity rows together, because that's the lesson in one glance. In maturity she sells more buns than in growth and makes less money doing it.What happened in between? In growth, her bigger volumes let her buy flour and butter in bulk from her supplier at a better price, and 90 buns come out of a single baking session. By maturity, two nearby cafés have copied her, so £3.00 stops working and she drops to £2.60 to hold her spot. She also pays for a new display case and a month of local advertising. Sales are at their highest; profit is quietly going backwards.And it all started with six weeks of recipe testing in development, when the buns sold nothing at all.
Photo by RDNE Stock project on PexelsThe four-stage curve is a pattern, not a law. Real products take several shapes, and mistaking one for another causes expensive mistakes: The fad — a sharp spike and a fast collapse. It never reaches maturity because it was never really about the product; it was about being in on something. If you build a factory for a fad, you own a factory. The fashion — a gentler rise, a real plateau, a gradual fade. Clothing styles, restaurant trends, most "healthy eating" waves. The classic — a long, long maturity, sometimes decades. Bread. Bicycles. A well-run corner shop. These are the ones that pay the bills. The stillborn — a product that never gets past introduction, usually because it solved a problem nobody had, or was priced wrong, or nobody ever heard of it. Two practical points fall out of this. First, the type of product shapes the cycle — a fashion item lives its whole life in months, while a durable tool can sit in maturity for a generation. Second, some products get a second life. Vinyl records were written off as dead and came back as a premium product for a different buyer. A product in decline is not always a product at the end.

Photo by https://kaboompics.com/ on PexelsNothing in strategy says you have to accept the curve as it arrives. Before you let a product slide into decline, you have four levers — and they're not mutually exclusive:A bakery example of each: selling buns to a café wholesale (new market), promoting them as an after-school snack as well as a breakfast (new use), launching a mini four-pack (product change), or going premium with a hand-rolled, slow-proved version at twice the price (repositioning).Two honest cautions. Extension costs money and, more importantly, it costs management attention — those are the scarce resources from the opening chapter, and every one spent reviving an old product is one not spent on a new one. And a product you keep alive out of sentiment is not a strategy; it's a bill. Read the signals, not the sales figures. Watch competitor entries, repeat-purchase rates, your own price resistance and the trade press. These are the controlling half of the management loop — the check that tells you a stage is turning before the accounts do. Invest ahead of the stage, not after it. Order the second oven while you're still in growth, because you'll wait six weeks for it. Add the extra delivery van, hire the driver, and expand into the wholesale channel before the queue forms. That's planning and organizing, and it's where most product launches are won or lost. Match your other factors to the stage. Distribution widens as you move from introduction to growth; customer service costs climb in maturity as everyone expects support; staffing needs shift from flexible all-rounders to specialists; suppliers get squeezed for better terms once your volumes justify it. The product cycle pulls every other chapter along with it. Mind the cash. Growth eats cash — stock, capacity, credit given to wholesale customers. Maturity throws it off. That's why a healthy company runs a portfolio of products at different stages, with the mature ones funding the launches. Don't kill a cash cow because it looks boring. A mature product with thin margins may still be paying your rent and bringing customers through the door who then buy other things. Equally, don't cling to a product that's genuinely finished. The question is never "is this old?" — it's "does the money and attention this product consumes earn more here than somewhere else?" The product life cycle runs through development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline — and it's really a story about rivals arriving as your product succeeds. Profit usually peaks before sales do, because unit costs stop falling, rivals force prices down, and selling gets more expensive. The curve is a pattern, not a law: fads spike and collapse, fashions plateau and fade, classics stay mature for decades, and some products die at introduction or come back years later. You can extend a cycle with new markets, new uses, product changes and repositioning — but every extension costs money and management attention. Use the cycle to plan ahead: build capacity and channels before the growth surge, not during it, and check the signals like any other control loop. Run a portfolio — mature products generate the cash that funds the growth products of tomorrow. A product's stage should never be a surprise. If it is, the failure isn't in the product; it's in the managing.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
